title: {{NAME}} and the Moongrass Match at the End of the Rainbow
moral: When you play with your whole heart and cheer for others as loudly as yourself, every game becomes something magical.

pages.content:
The rainbow did not fade after the storm as rainbows are supposed to do. It stayed, anchored at both ends in the meadow behind the school, and as the afternoon light shifted from gold to amber, {{NAME}} could see something extraordinary happening along its arc.

The rainbow was a road. Beings were walking it.

Unicorns trotted in single file along the violet band, their hooves ringing like coins dropped on glass. Fairies zipped in organized formations through the indigo and blue, clutching tiny pennants and arguing at spectacular volume about formations. At the far end, the rainbow curved down to a pitch of moongrass, pale and shimmering, where goalposts grew like silver saplings from the earth.

The pitch sat inside a valley {{NAME}} had never noticed before, secret and hushed, ringed by the dark shapes of the surrounding hills. The grass caught every colour from the rainbow above and held it, so the whole field glowed with soft, shifting light.

A fairy in a coral-coloured kit shot down from the nearest archway and hovered in front of {{NAME}}'s nose. 'You're here about the match?' she demanded.

'I didn't know there was a match,' {{NAME}} said honestly.

'Wonderful,' said the fairy. 'We need a goalkeeper. Ours ate too many moonberries and is currently luminous.'

pages.content:
The fairy's name was Floss, and she had opinions about everything.

She had opinions about footwork, about the correct angle at which a goalkeeper should set their feet, about whether the moongrass was slightly longer on the left flank than the right, and about a unicorn named Cosmo who was apparently a brilliant striker but had a tendency to celebrate goals with a display of sparkle that temporarily blinded the opposing defenders.

'We have a rule about that,' Floss said, shaking a finger at Cosmo as she introduced them. 'No sparkle until the referee's whistle.'

Cosmo looked genuinely sorry, which was impressive given that he was a unicorn the size of a large pony, radiantly white with a rose-gold horn and eyes the warm amber of autumn leaves.

{{NAME}} looked at Cosmo. Cosmo looked at {{NAME}}. Then Cosmo lowered his head and very gently bumped his velvet nose against {{NAME}}'s cheek, which settled something immediately.

'He does that when he decides someone is good,' Floss said, her expression softening despite her best efforts to maintain strictness. 'He's only wrong once. Ever. And that was a beetle, and beetles are tricky to read.'

{{NAME}} reached up and scratched behind Cosmo's rose-gold horn. Cosmo's eyes went half-closed with pleasure. The moongrass around their feet lit up brighter, as if agreeing with everyone.

pages.content:
The match was played under a sky that cycled slowly through every colour it knew.

{{NAME}} had never kept goal before, not properly, but the moongrass had a way of whispering to your feet, telling them where to move a half-second before you'd worked it out yourself. He dived left and caught a shot that should have been a goal. He punched clear a corner that Floss had curled with frightening accuracy. He shouted encouragement so often that by halftime his voice had turned raspy and warm.

Cosmo, playing centre forward, was a revelation. He moved the ball between his front hooves with improbable delicacy, weaving between defenders, and when he struck for goal he did so with the precision of someone who had thought about that exact moment for a long time.

His first goal: Cosmo cut inside from the left, let a fairy defender commit, and slotted the ball into the bottom corner with his right hoof. Clean. Perfect.

The second goal: Cosmo received the ball from Floss at the edge of the area and, instead of shooting, held it for one impossible second while {{NAME}} sprinted sixty metres, arriving at the far post just as Cosmo's perfectly weighted chip floated overhead.

{{NAME}} did not have to head it. He did not have to do anything. He just had to be there. But Cosmo had known he would be.

pages.content:
With the score at two goals apiece and seconds remaining, something went wrong.

Cosmo fell.

Not a tackle, not a foul. Simply, mid-run, his legs folded beneath him, and he lay on the moongrass with his rose-gold horn pressed to the ground and his breathing too fast and too shallow.

'Cosmo!' Floss was beside him in an instant, her tiny hands pressing against his flank, her face stripped of all her usual bossiness, leaving something rawer underneath.

The fairies from both teams landed on the pitch simultaneously. The referee, a very old fairy with wings like cracked parchment, raised her whistle but did not blow it.

{{NAME}} ran.

He had no plan. He simply ran to where Cosmo was, and he sat down in the moongrass beside that great white head and placed his hand just below the rose-gold horn, where the warmth radiated most strongly.

'Easy,' he said softly. 'I've got you. Easy.'

Cosmo's breathing slowed. His amber eyes focused. Around them the moongrass glowed with gentle, steadying light, the whole pitch concentrated into this one small warm circle of it.

Floss looked at {{NAME}} from the other side of Cosmo's neck, her expression complicated and grateful and entirely unguarded.

'He just needed someone to stay,' she said quietly.

'I know,' said {{NAME}}.

pages.content:
Cosmo was back on his feet within minutes, stiff-legged and a little embarrassed, which apparently unicorns express through excessive snorting.

They replayed the final seconds. Cosmo, who was supposed to take the deciding shot, passed instead to Floss, who looked astonished, then composed herself in roughly a quarter of a second and knocked the ball precisely into the top corner.

Floss's whole team erupted. {{NAME}} jumped so high that two fairies had to grab his collar to keep him from rising altogether.

The rainbow began to fade at last, gently, the way good things end when they are ready rather than when they are forced. The moongrass dimmed from silver to a comfortable green. The unicorns trotted back toward the hills in the last soft light, Cosmo pausing at the edge to look back at {{NAME}} one more time.

That look, {{NAME}} decided, was worth remembering for a very long time.

He walked home under a wide plain sky, cold and clear, the feel of Cosmo's warmth still on his palm.

He was almost asleep when he heard the sound, delicate and unmistakable, of fairy pennants snapping in a distant wind.

And a voice, tiny as a dewdrop, called: 'Same time next rainbow, goalkeeper.'
